Stage 6: the world model decides which driver gets which rider

World model 3 · ride_world · San Francisco and Pune

Every 30 seconds a ride platform must decide which free driver goes to which waiting rider (matching), and every 5 minutes which idle drivers it should send to areas where riders are expected (repositioning). Normally a hand-written rule does both: the closest driver gets the rider, and drivers are nudged towards busy areas. In stage 5 the world model learned to do the repositioning. In stage 6 it also does the matching, and its decisions are carried out in the real simulator.

In short
  • It matches as well as the platform's rule. With the same repositioning, its own matching changed the reward by −1.1 ± 3.9 in San Francisco and +0.3 ± 5.5 in Pune: no difference beyond noise.
  • Drivers rejected fewer of its offers: about 11 fewer per 2 hours in San Francisco and 19 fewer in Pune.
  • It learned by copying the rule inside the world model's imagination (it picks exactly the rule's driver 86-90% of the time). Extra reinforcement learning on matching did not improve it further.
  • Building on the pretrained world model pays: the same network trained from scratch earns 11 reward less in San Francisco (+11.3 ± 3.5, better on 15 of 20 days).
  • In Pune nothing beats "do nothing" clearly; the rule's small edge there comes from its repositioning, not its matching.

How the agent was made

1. Imaginethe world model replays the city from 144 real starting moments per city
→
2. Copy the rulein imagination, every waiting rider learns to pick the same driver the rule would pick (15k choices SF, 26k Pune)
→
3. Try to improvereinforcement learning (GRPO): try other drivers for one rider, keep what earns more reward 20 min later
→
4. Run for realthe agent decides inside the simulator on unseen days, 12:00-14:00 (20 SF + 12 Pune days)
→
5. Comparesame days with the platform's rule, and with no repositioning

    The figures, explained

    Carried out in the simulator: every decision maker on unseen days

    What it shows

    • Top row San Francisco, bottom row Pune. Each panel is one measure over the 2-hour window, as a difference from the rule's matching with no repositioning.
    • Bars = mean over days, with standard error; black dots = individual days; open diamonds = what the world model imagined for the same decision maker.
    • rule = platform's rule; stage 5 = rule matches, agent repositions; IM-p = agent does both, pretrained; IM-s = agent does both, from scratch.

    What to take from it

    • San Francisco: the pretrained agent (dark orange) reaches the rule's reward and pickups; the scratch agent (green) gets about half.
    • Offers rejected: the pretrained agent's offers are turned down less often than the rule's.
    • Pickup minutes of offers and rider waits barely move: matching closest-first is already near the best; the agent learned to do the same.
    • Pune: all bars sit within the scatter of the dots: no decision maker clearly helps there in 2 hours.
    • Diamonds close to bars mean the world model predicted these effects well before anything was run.

    Step 2: copying the rule's matching in imagination

    What it shows

    • Training curves over 6 passes through the data; dark orange = built on the pretrained world model, green = from scratch.
    • 1st column: how surprised the agent is by the rule's choice (lower is better). 2nd: how often it picks exactly the rule's driver.
    • 3rd: pickup minutes of the driver it picks vs the rule's (dashed). 4th: how far its repositioning drifted from stage 5 (should stay near 0).

    What to take from it

    • After one pass the agent already picks the rule's driver ~85% (SF) / ~89% (Pune) of the time, and when it differs it picks a driver just as close (2.0 vs 1.96 min SF).
    • Its repositioning is unchanged (drift below 0.02), so stage 6 adds matching without losing stage 5.

    Step 3: trying to improve matching with reinforcement learning (in imagination)

    What it shows

    • 40 iterations of GRPO; each point is the imagined reward over 60 minutes from held-out starting moments, compared with rule matching and no repositioning.
    • Solid = the stage-6 agent; dotted = stage-5 agent (rule matches); dashed blue = the platform's rule. Last column: how often the agent chooses to hold a rider back.

    What to take from it

    • The solid line does not climb: SF +4.2 → +4.3, Pune +0.4 → −2.3. Reinforcement learning found nothing better than closest-first.
    • Why: once matching is closest-first, which of two nearby drivers gets one rider changes little an hour later; the gains are in where idle drivers wait (stage 5).
    • The imitation agent (before RL) is therefore the one carried out in the simulator above.
